r-9.4-develop-team.title: 9.4 Develop Team: high-performing team behaviours, Tuckman ladder, colocation, team building, recognition, training, assessments
r-9.4-develop-team.notes: Improve competencies, team interaction and the team environment; key benefit: improved teamwork, interpersonal skills and competencies, motivated employees, reduced attrition, better performance; performed throughout. Developing effective teams is a primary PM responsibility: create an environment for teamwork; motivate with challenges and opportunities, timely feedback and support, recognition and rewards. High performance via open and effective communication, team-building opportunities, trust, constructive conflict management, collaborative problem solving and decision making. Global, culturally diverse teams (multiple languages, a 'team language'): capitalise on cultural differences, sustain the team, work interdependently with mutual trust. Objectives: improve knowledge and skills (lower cost, shorter schedule, better quality); improve trust and agreement (morale up, conflict down, more teamwork); create a dynamic, cohesive, collaborative culture (productivity, spirit, cross-training and mentoring); empower the team to make decisions and own solutions. Tuckman ladder - five stages, usually in order but teams can get stuck, regress or skip if they worked together before: forming (meet, learn roles; independent and less open), storming (address work, technical decisions and approach; can be counterproductive without openness), norming (adjust habits to support the team; trust develops), performing (well-organised, interdependent, resolve issues smoothly), adjourning (work done, team released, e.g., at Close Project or Phase); stage length depends on dynamics, size and leadership. Inputs: resource management plan (rewards, feedback, training, discipline, team performance assessment criteria); documents (lessons learned, project schedule - when to train and build competencies, project team assignments, resource calendars - when members can join development activities, team charter); EEFs (HR policies - hiring, termination, reviews, training records, recognition; team skills and knowledge; geographic distribution); OPAs (historical information, lessons learned). Tools: colocation (place the most active members in one location - temporary or whole project; team meeting room, shared schedule boards - sometimes called a 'war room' in practice, though the Guide doesn't use that term here); virtual teams (more skilled resources, lower cost, less travel and relocation, proximity to suppliers or customers; online team environment with file storage, threads, calendar); communication technology (shared portal, video conferencing, audio conferencing, email/chat); interpersonal and team skills - conflict management (timely and constructive), influencing (gather relevant information, reach agreement while keeping trust), motivation (providing a reason to act; empower decision making and independent work), negotiation (consensus on project needs), team building (activities that enhance social relations and cooperation, from a 5-minute agenda item to a facilitated offsite; valuable for remote teams; essential early but continuous); recognition and rewards (plan made in Plan Resource Management; effective only if they satisfy a need the individual values; consider culture; intangible rewards can be as effective as money - growth, accomplishment, appreciation, challenge; recognise throughout, not just at the end); training (formal or informal: classroom, online, computer-based, on-the-job, mentoring, coaching; scheduled per the resource plan or unplanned after observation and appraisals; cost may be in the project budget or borne by the organisation if skills are reusable); individual and team assessments (attitudinal surveys, specific assessments, structured interviews, ability tests, focus groups - preferences, aspirations, information processing, decision making, interaction; build understanding, trust, commitment, communication); meetings (orientation, team-building, team development). Outputs: team performance assessments (formal or informal; indicators - improved individual skills, improved team competencies, reduced turnover, increased cohesiveness; identify training, coaching, mentoring, assistance or changes and the resources needed); change requests; plan updates (resource management plan); document updates (lessons learned, project schedule, project team assignments, resource calendars, team charter); EEF updates (employee development plan records, skill assessments); OPA updates (training requirements, personnel assessment).

r-9.5-manage-team.title: 9.5 Manage Team: conflict sources and five resolution techniques, decision making, emotional intelligence, influencing, leadership
r-9.5-manage-team.notes: Track team member performance, give feedback, resolve issues and manage team changes; key benefit: influences behaviour, manages conflict, resolves issues; performed throughout. Requires management and leadership skills with emphasis on communication, conflict management, negotiation and leadership; give challenging assignments and recognition; adapt style to members' willingness and ability (low-skill members need more intensive oversight). Inputs: resource management plan (how team resources are managed and released); documents (issue log - who resolves what by when; lessons learned; project team assignments; team charter - how the team decides, meets, resolves conflict); work performance reports (from schedule control, cost control, quality control and scope validation - inform resource needs, rewards and plan updates); team performance assessments (ongoing, to resolve issues, modify communication, address conflict, improve interaction); EEFs (HR policies); OPAs (certificates of appreciation, corporate apparel, other perquisites). Tools: interpersonal and team skills - conflict management: conflict is inevitable; sources include scarce resources, scheduling priorities and personal work styles; ground rules, group norms, communication planning and role definition reduce it; managed well it increases creativity and better decisions; team members are initially responsible for resolving their conflicts; if it escalates, the PM facilitates; address early, usually in private, directly and collaboratively; persistent disruptive conflict may need formal procedures including discipline. Factors in choosing a method: importance and intensity, time pressure, relative power, importance of the relationship, motivation for a long- or short-term solution. Five techniques: withdraw/avoid (retreat or postpone to prepare or let others resolve); smooth/accommodate (emphasise agreement, concede to maintain harmony); compromise/reconcile (some satisfaction for all, temporary or partial; occasionally lose-lose); force/direct (push one view at others' expense, win-lose, usually via power to resolve an emergency); collaborate/problem solve (incorporate multiple viewpoints, cooperative attitude and open dialogue leading to consensus and commitment; can be win-win). Decision making (here the ability to negotiate and influence; guidelines: focus on goals, follow a process, study environmental factors, analyse information, stimulate creativity, account for risk). Emotional intelligence (identify, assess and manage one's own, others' and groups' emotions; reduce tension, increase cooperation, anticipate actions, acknowledge concerns, follow up issues). Influencing (critical in a matrix with little direct authority: persuasiveness, clear articulation, active and effective listening, awareness of perspectives, gathering information while maintaining trust). Leadership (lead and inspire the team throughout the life cycle; use styles suited to situation; communicate the vision). PMIS (resource or scheduling software to coordinate members). Outputs: change requests (e.g., staffing changes - reassignments, outsourcing, replacing leavers - can cause schedule slips or overruns); plan updates (resource management plan, schedule baseline, cost baseline); document updates (issue log, lessons learned, project team assignments); EEF updates (input to organisational performance appraisals, personnel skill). Data flow: work performance reports from 4.5; team performance assessments from 9.4; change requests to 4.6.

r-9.6-control-resources.title: 9.6 Control Resources: physical resource control, problem-solving steps, outputs
r-9.6-control-resources.notes: Ensure physical resources assigned and allocated are available as planned, monitor planned vs actual utilisation and take corrective action; key benefit: resources available at the right time and place and released when no longer needed; performed continuously in all phases. Concerns physical resources (equipment, materials, facilities, infrastructure) - team members are handled in Manage Team. Concerned with: monitoring resource expenditures; identifying and dealing with shortage/surplus in time; using and releasing resources per plan; informing stakeholders of issues; influencing factors that change utilisation; managing actual changes. Schedule or cost baseline changes only via Perform Integrated Change Control. Inputs: resource management plan; documents (issue log - lack of resources, delayed or low-grade raw material; lessons learned; physical resource assignments - expected utilisation, type, amount, location, internal or outsourced; project schedule; RBS - reference for replacing or reacquiring; resource requirements; risk register); work performance data (number and type of resources used); agreements (basis for all external resources; define procedures for new unplanned resources or issues); OPAs (resource control and assignment policies, escalation procedures, lessons learned). Tools: data analysis - alternatives analysis (e.g., pay overtime or add resources vs late or phased delivery), cost-benefit analysis, performance reviews (planned vs actual utilisation; cost and schedule information), trend analysis (resources needed for upcoming stages); problem solving - problems from inside (machines not released by another department, materials damaged by bad storage) or outside (supplier bankruptcy, weather damage); steps: identify the problem, define it (break into smaller problems), investigate (collect data), analyse (find root cause), solve (choose a suitable solution), check the solution; interpersonal skills - negotiation (additional or changed physical resources, costs), influencing; PMIS (monitor utilisation - right resources on right activities at the right time and place). Outputs: work performance information (requirements and allocation vs utilisation; availability gaps); change requests; plan updates (resource management plan, schedule baseline, cost baseline); document updates (assumption log, issue log, lessons learned - logistics, scrap, utilisation variances, corrective actions; physical resource assignments - dynamic; RBS; risk register). Data flow: WPD from 4.3; agreements from 12.2; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

m-communications-intro.title: Project Communications Management: purpose, two parts, three processes
m-communications-intro.notes: Ensure information needs of the project and stakeholders are met by developing artefacts and implementing activities for effective information exchange. Two parts: developing a communication strategy that is effective for stakeholders, and carrying out activities to implement it. Processes: 10.1 Plan Communications Management (develop an approach and plan based on each stakeholder's or group's information needs, organisational assets and project needs); 10.2 Manage Communications (timely and appropriate collection, creation, distribution, storage, retrieval, management, monitoring and ultimate disposition of project information); 10.3 Monitor Communications (ensure information needs of the project and stakeholders are met). (Overview continues on PDF 397.)
